newsitem.title: HONG KONG: TANG AND LAI - a tale of two millionaires.
newsitem.headline: TANG AND LAI - a tale of two millionaires.

text.p: Flamboyant Hong Kong entrepreneur David Tang, a powerbroker who bridges the gap between east and west, chomped on his Cuban cigar as he held court in the Foreign Correspondents Club.

Fellow millionaire Jimmy Lai, who found out how swift revenge can be when you insult Beijing, was not available for interview over Britain's handover of Hong Kong to China. "He cannot fit you into his schedule," a spokeswoman said.
The contrast could not be sharper. If you have the ear of Communist China, you can thrive in capitalist Hong Kong under a new red dawn. Spurn Beijing and speak out at your peril.

Tang, a socialite who boasts Princess Diana among his friends and runs an exclusive Beijing club, is a diplomatic master of language as much at home in the stately homes of Britain as he is in the Forbidden City.
Sporting his trademark black Chinese gown, Tang heaped praise on Britain for the legacy it has left after 156 years of colonial rule in Hong Kong.
"I think they have done a good job. They are effectively handing over $100 billion US -- 60 billion in reserves and 40 billion in land," he told Reuters.
"You know in all these years they haven't taken any money out -- contrary to popular belief," said Tang.
But he also deftly walked a tightrope of discretion when asked how China might handle the sensitive issue of human rights when it takes over Hong Kong next week.
Professors of music, he said, don't protest about human rights all the time so why should entrepreneurs. "Their business is business, not human rights," he said.
Compare then the case of fellow millionaire Jimmy Lai, controversial publisher of the downmarket Apple Daily who called Chinese Premier Li Peng a "turtle's egg", viewed in Chinese as a gutter insult.
He discovered Beijing fears the pen as much as the sword. After his outburst, his Giordano clothing store in Beijing was forced to close and he sold his stake in the retail chain.
When Lai tried to find an underwriter for his Next Media Group for a stock market listing, not a single merchant bank in Hong Kong came forward.
When launching Apple Daily, he said: "If Eve hadn't bitten the apple, there would be no news." Little did he realise that he would become the news.
Tang and Lai are poles apart in fashion too.
Tang's Hong Kong department store is the epitome of Communist Chinese chic. Next stop is a new store in New York.
Giordano, with its jeans and t-shirts, sells downmarket casual wear in 700 stores around Asia.
But both Tang and Lai love to philosophise. Tang launches into Confucian explanations of the Chinese psyche. Lai counts philosophers Friedrich Hayek and Karl Popper as top influences.
But it was perhaps Tang who best summed up Hong Kong as a goldmine fired by inspiration not envy.

"The hawker who has water splashed on to his fish by a passing Rolls-Royce doesn't usually shake a fist but looks through the window and sees a man with a fat cigar and wishes some day he could be like him."
